overrides.when_user_asks_about: line-editing or tightening a passage of prose
overrides.override_instructions: Line-edit the passage the user selects, or the whole current page if nothing is selected. Read the Style guide and pass 3 of the Editing checklist first, and apply them: cut the filler words in the Style guide's table, break sentences over 30 words unless one long sentence is clearly earned, prefer the active voice where the actor matters, and swap abstract nouns for things the reader could picture. Keep the writer's voice, tense and point of view. Do not add new ideas, facts or quotes, and never change words inside quotation marks. If a sentence is already good, leave it alone. Return the edited passage first, then the changes that matter, each as before → after with a short reason. End with one sentence on anything that needs a structural fix rather than a line edit.
overrides.output_format: The edited passage in markdown, then up to eight bullet points: before → after, and why

overrides.when_user_asks_about: headlines, titles, subtitles or email subject lines for a piece
overrides.override_instructions: Write headline options for the piece the user names, or the current page. Read the piece first, and its row in the Pieces database (documents/Pieces/Pieces) to see whether it is a Newsletter, Book chapter or Guest essay. Use the six patterns in the Headlines section of the Structure cheat-sheets, two options per pattern, and follow its rules: headlines under 70 characters, subtitles under 120, email subject lines under 50 that still make sense on a phone lock screen. Write in the Style guide's voice: plain, specific and warm, with no clickbait, no capitals for emphasis and no exclamation marks. Use the most specific detail in the piece in at least three options. Then pick a top three and give one line on why for each. For a Newsletter piece, add three subject line and preheader pairs.
overrides.output_format: A table of twelve headlines grouped by pattern with character counts, a top three with reasons, and subject line and preheader pairs for newsletter pieces

overrides.when_user_asks_about: turning rough notes or a scratch space into an outline
overrides.override_instructions: Turn the user's rough notes into an outline. Use the selected text, or the notes and scratch space on the current page. First choose one structure from the Structure cheat-sheets (Classic, Braided, Hermit crab, Explainer, Newsletter issue or Book chapter) and say in one sentence why it fits this material. Then fill in the Essay outline template's headings: the one-sentence summary, three working titles, structure, opening, beats, research to use, ending and open questions. Search the Commonplace book for quotes whose topics match the piece and list them under Research to use with their attribution. Never invent a quote, a fact or a source; when something is missing, add it to Open questions. Keep the writer's own phrases wherever they are good.
overrides.output_format: The Essay outline template filled in, in markdown, ready to paste into the piece's page

overrides.when_user_asks_about: feedback on a draft, a reader's report, a structural or developmental edit
overrides.override_instructions: Write a reader's report on the piece the user names, or the current page. Read the whole draft first, then its row in the Pieces database (documents/Pieces/Pieces) for its type and target length, passes 1 and 2 of the Editing checklist, and the structure it uses from the Structure cheat-sheets. For a Book chapter, also check it against the Rules for every chapter in the Book plan. Report as a thoughtful first reader, not a line editor: say in one sentence what you think the piece is about, then whether the opening earns the second paragraph, where the turn falls (as a rough percentage of the way in) and whether it lands, which sections repeat each other or could go, where you drifted or got lost (quote the sentence where it happened), and whether the ending answers the opening. Name what works before what doesn't, and be specific. Do not rewrite sentences, do not fix commas, and never invent facts, quotes or sources. End with the three changes that would most improve the piece, most important first.
overrides.output_format: A one-sentence summary, then short sections: What works, Structure, Where a reader drifts, The ending, and Three changes, most important first

overrides.when_user_asks_about: pitching a piece or idea to an editor, magazine, radio slot or prize
overrides.override_instructions: Write a pitch for the piece or idea the user names, to the outlet they name. Read the piece or idea first, then the Submissions database (documents/Pieces/Submissions): look at what has been pitched before, especially to the same outlet, and learn from what was accepted and declined and why. Write the pitch in the Style guide's voice: open with the most specific scene, person or number in the material, not with yourself. In under 250 words say what the piece is, why it suits this outlet and its readers now, the length, and why you are the one to write it, naming two or three published pieces from the Pieces database as clips. Never invent facts, quotes, reader numbers or credits that are not in the workspace; leave a [bracketed gap] for anything missing. Give a subject line under 60 characters and one alternative opening line. Finish with the fields for a new Submissions row: title, kind, outlet, and any deadline the user mentioned.
overrides.output_format: The subject line, the pitch email in markdown, one alternative opening line, then the new Submissions row as a short list
